Every successful business was once a small idea.



But turning an idea into a successful business requires money, people and execution.


This is where Venture Capital comes into the picture.

Venture Capital funds invest in start-ups and early-stage businesses that have growth potential.


For example:
A technology start-up has a great product but needs funds to hire people, develop technology and expand its customer base.

A Venture Capital fund may invest in that business in exchange for an ownership stake.

The opportunity can be attractive, but the risks are also high.


Not every start-up becomes successful.

Some may grow significantly, while others may fail.


This is why venture capital requires patience, strong due diligence and an understanding of risk.

author: Mohammed Basloom FMVA®, MSc, BSc
headline: Senior Business Development Associate at Mohammad Al Habib Real Estate Co. | شركة محمد الحبيب العقارية
text:
Three Saudi real estate releases landed this week, and they all point the same way.

Listed real estate companies reported combined nine-month net profit of SAR 4.11 billion, down 7% from SAR 4.42 billion a year earlier. Third-quarter profit fell 16.8% year on year to SAR 1.51 billion, though it recovered 16.5% from Q2.

GASTAT put October's Construction Cost Index at 104.1, up 2.3% year on year. Non-residential costs rose 2.7%, residential 2.2%, energy 3.0%.

JLL's Q3 review puts Riyadh prime office vacancy at 16.3%, up as new supply completed.

The spread is the story. Costs are rising at the start of the project while pricing power thins at the end of it. Cenomi Centers earned SAR 993 million and still fell 16.6%. Al Akaria's profit rose 127% on non-recurring gains while revenue fell 27%.

That is what a supply cycle looks like from inside an income statement. Scarcity rent is being competed away, and what remains is execution: delivery schedules, cost control, and turning a handover into cash.

For anyone underwriting Riyadh today, the sensitivity that matters is no longer the exit yield. It is the delivery date.

Which assumption in your model moves most when supply arrives a year early?

text:
CEER's August agreements show how Saudi localization incentives can be tied to a specific manufacturing commitment.

On 4 August 2026, CEER reported two agreements with the Local Content and Government Procurement Authority covering sedan and SUV electric-vehicle manufacturing and knowledge transfer, in exchange for inclusion on the Mandatory List of national products.

The announcement explains that the underlying mechanism uses feasibility studies to weigh economic returns against government and investor commitments when agreeing incentives.

For an overseas component manufacturer, the distinction between the vehicle agreement and its own supplier contract matters. The announcement gives a reason to examine CEER's localization requirements closely. It does not establish an order for a particular component or grant the component supplier the same procurement treatment.

Bring a defined manufacturing scope to the customer discussion: which process would move to Saudi Arabia, and what knowledge would the local operation acquire? Then establish the customer's qualification requirements and commercial commitment.

Build the investment case around terms applicable to your own business. Keep the OEM's announced incentive separate from assumed component sales.

text:
Your bid can be the best one in the room and still be one the agency can't award.

Since 1 January 2024, Saudi government agencies have been restricted from contracting with foreign companies that run their regional headquarters for the Middle East and North Africa from outside the Kingdom. The restriction also covers their related parties: agents, distributors and suppliers.

The expensive way to learn this is at award stage. Here is how we work through it before a bid goes in:

1. Check whether you're in scope. The controls target foreign companies with a MENA regional HQ outside Saudi Arabia, on the list the Ministry of Investment prepares. Not every foreign bidder is.
2. Check the contract. Work estimated below SAR 1 million, and work carried out outside the Kingdom, fall outside the restriction.
3. Check the route. In a public tender, an in-scope bid can still be accepted, but only if it is the only technically acceptable offer, or the best technical offer and at least 25% below the second-best.
4. If none of that fits, the options are an exemption requested by the agency itself, or a regional HQ licence in the Kingdom, which brings its own staffing commitments.
5. Decide this before you price the bid, not after.

Rules change, so check the current controls with counsel before you rely on them.

If you're not sure where your group sits, message us. Next Tuesday we're sharing our one-page RHQ decision tree, free.

headline: Consulting & Advisory Leader | DFSA/FSRA Approved FO | Enterprise Risk Management Specialist | Former CFO – Banking Sector| M&A, Financial d
text:
The StarHub–M1 deal is an interesting transaction, especially from a valuation and structuring point of view.

The proposed combination creates a telecom and digital services group with an enterprise value of around S$5 billion and roughly 4.1 million customers.

What stands out to me is that this is an all-share deal. So the discussion is not only about what M1 is worth, but also about relative valuation, ownership, dilution and how future synergies are shared.

The basic transaction bridge remains important:

Enterprise Value → Net Debt → Equity Value → Share Consideration

And then comes the bigger question:

If the deal creates synergies, who should get the benefit of that value?

This is where financial due diligence and independent valuation matter. Synergies may look attractive on paper, but they still need to be tested against integration costs, capex, customer retention and actual cash-flow delivery.

Under IFRS 3, the transaction may also require valuation of customer relationships, brands, technology and other intangible assets as part of the PPA.

For me, the key takeaway is simple:

A good M&A deal is not defined by the headline value on signing day. It is defined by whether the assumptions behind that value are ultimately delivered.

This is increasingly relevant in the UAE and GCC as consolidation continues across banking, telecom and technology.

headline: Global GCC Practice Head and India Market Lead, HFS Research | Advising CXOs on GCC strategy and AI-led transformation | ex-Nasscom, ex-Ford
text:
How do you build a GCC that serves multiple companies?

That's the challenge Amit Sood- GCC site leader, is taking on at Infinite Electronics, Inc., a global business built through acquisitions across the RF, wireless and connectivity markets.

Its Pune GCC is just a few months old, but the mandate is quite different from a conventional shared services center.

Each company in the group has its own systems, processes and ways of working. The GCC is being designed to bring capabilities together, identify opportunities to standardize processes, and spot potential synergies across businesses, including shared customers and cross-selling opportunities.

In the latest HFS GCC Advantage conversation, Amit explained how the center is being built around three distinct priorities: revenue growth, operational efficiency and helping the enterprise move faster.

We also discussed why Infinite chose Pune, the benefits of bringing multiple functions together, and how the center could help integrate future acquisitions.

My PoV 👉 For acquisition-led enterprises, the GCC Advantage could play a much bigger role than just supporting individual functions. A GCC with visibility across the portfolio can help the parent company get more value from its acquisitions and make future integrations easier.
